faqs.answer: 16 g of coarse coffee per 240 ml mug at 1:15. A 34 oz press takes about 67 g of coffee and a litre of water.
faqs.question: How much coffee do I put in a French press?

faqs.answer: Usually the coffee sat on the grounds too long. Press after four minutes and pour it all out straight away. Coffee left in the press keeps extracting and turns bitter.
faqs.question: Why is my French press coffee bitter?

faqs.answer: Coarse, like breadcrumbs. Fine grounds slip through the mesh into the cup and make the plunger hard to push.
faqs.question: What grind should I use for French press?

faqs.answer: About four real mugs. A French press cup is about 4 oz, so an 8-cup press holds around a litre, which is four 8 oz mugs.
faqs.question: How many cups does an 8-cup French press make?

faqs.answer: Use wood or plastic. A metal spoon can chip a glass carafe, and a chipped carafe can break when it is full of hot coffee. Bodum recalled millions of presses for exactly this reason.
faqs.question: Can I use a metal spoon to stir?

felicityNote: The press is my lazy-morning brewer: coarse grounds, four minutes, done. The one rule I never break is pouring it all out the moment I press.

parts.meaning: The ground coffee in grams, weighed before brewing.
The grams of water for each gram of coffee at the 1:15 starting ratio.
The water in grams. One millilitre of water weighs one gram, so grams and ml are the same number.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the coffee and water
howToSteps.text: Use 16 g of coarse coffee for a 240 ml mug, or scale up at 1:15. A litre of water takes 67 g of coffee.

howToSteps.name: Add the coffee, then the water
howToSteps.text: Put the grounds in the press. Pour water at about 93 C over them, stir once with a wooden or plastic spoon, and put the lid on with the plunger up.

howToSteps.name: Wait four minutes
howToSteps.text: Let the coffee steep for four minutes. Do not press yet. The grounds need the full time to give up their flavour.

howToSteps.name: Press and pour
howToSteps.text: Push the plunger down slowly and steadily. Pour the coffee straight away. Coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps brewing and turns bitter.

lede: French press starts at 1:15, one gram of coffee for every 15 grams of water. That is 16 g of coarse-ground coffee for a 240 ml mug, steeped for four minutes.

title: French Press Coffee to Water Ratio
tutorial: French press is immersion brewing: the grounds sit in the water for the whole brew, instead of water passing through them. That is why the ratio is a little stronger than pour-over. Start at 1:15, one gram of coffee for every 15 grams of water, which is 16 g of coffee for a 240 ml mug.

The National Coffee Association gives a wider range, 1:10 to 1:16, and the Specialty Coffee Association's batch-brewing figure sits at the lighter end. In practice most French press guides land on 1:15. Go to 1:13 or 1:14 for a bolder cup, or 1:16 to 1:17 for something lighter and closer to filter coffee.

Grind coarse, like breadcrumbs. Fine grounds slip through the mesh and end up in the cup, and they make the plunger hard to push. Coarse grounds stay put, the plunger moves smoothly, and the coffee stays clean. If you have to force the plunger, the grind is too fine.

Water just off the boil is right: about 93 C, or 200 F. Let the kettle sit for 30 seconds after it clicks off. Pour the water over the grounds, stir once with a wooden or plastic spoon, put the lid on with the plunger up, and wait four minutes. Then press slowly and pour straight away, so the coffee stops brewing.

Watch the cup markings on the press. A French press cup is about 4 oz, so an 8-cup press holds about a litre and makes four real mugs, not eight. Weighing the water is the only way to be sure, and it is also how the ratio works: water in grams divided by 15 is the coffee in grams.
